title: Broker Decision Framework
description: Apply a structured framework to evaluate and select the right message broker for any system.

data.text: Choosing a message broker is rarely about picking the most popular one. It is about matching broker capabilities to your delivery requirements, team expertise, and operational constraints. A structured framework removes guesswork and makes the decision auditable.
Most broker decisions can be reduced to five questions. Answer each honestly before you reach for a specific technology. The answers will narrow your options far more than vendor marketing.

data.title: Five dimensions to evaluate
items: Delivery semantics: Do you need at-most-once, at-least-once, or exactly-once processing? Exactly-once often requires idempotent consumers regardless of broker choice.
Throughput and scale: How many messages per second must the system sustain? Kafka handles millions; RabbitMQ handles tens to hundreds of thousands on a single node.
Ordering requirements: Is per-key ordering critical? Kafka guarantees partition-level order. RabbitMQ guarantees queue-level order only with a single consumer.
Operational model: Can your team run a cluster, or do you need a managed service? SQS removes ops entirely; Kafka requires the most expertise.
Replay and retention: Do consumers ever need to re-read historical messages? Kafka supports long retention; SQS and RabbitMQ do not.

data.text: A simple scoring matrix helps teams compare brokers objectively. Rate each dimension from 1 (poor fit) to 5 (excellent fit), then sum the scores. The highest score is your starting point, not your final answer.

data.title: Broker scoring matrix in C#

data.text: Start by documenting your non-functional requirements: target throughput, maximum acceptable latency, ordering constraints, and who will operate the infrastructure. Next, score each broker on the five dimensions. Finally, verify your top choice against real-world failure modes—what happens when a consumer falls behind, when a node restarts, or when the network partitions?

data.caption: A repeatable framework for broker selection that turns subjective preferences into measurable decisions.

terms.definition: The contract for message delivery: at-most-once, at-least-once, or exactly-once.
A system requirement that describes how the system should behave, not what it should do (e.g., throughput, latency).

data.title: Common Bias
data.text: Teams often overweight operational familiarity. A broker your team already knows scores higher on operational model, but if it cannot meet your throughput or ordering requirements, familiarity is not a valid justification.

items.question: What if two brokers tie on the score?
items.answer: Run a time-boxed spike with real traffic patterns. Theoretical scores matter less than observed latency, error rates, and developer experience.

items.question: Should I include cost in the framework?
items.answer: Yes. Managed services have predictable pricing; self-hosted clusters have hidden costs in hardware, monitoring, and on-call time.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Evaluate brokers across five dimensions: delivery semantics, throughput, ordering, operations, and retention.
Use a scoring matrix to make comparisons objective and repeatable.
Always validate with a spike before committing to production.
Bias toward operational fit, not just feature checklists.
data.takeaway: A decision framework turns broker selection from a debate into a repeatable process that the whole team can trust.
